question: A company has negative contribution margins on every unit. It plans to 'grow into profitability' by scaling volume. Will this work?
before: If contribution margin (revenue minus variable costs per unit) is negative, you lose money on every sale BEFORE fixed costs. Scaling multiplies the per-unit loss. Fixed cost leverage only helps with positive contribution margin. Option D is misleading — successful startups had positive contribution margins; they were unprofitable due to fixed cost investments, not per-unit losses.
after:
Concept: Contribution margin is the revenue per unit minus variable cost per unit. It represents how much each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and profit. If contribution margin is negative, each unit sold generates a loss before any fixed costs are considered.

Why this is correct: When contribution margin is negative, every additional unit sold increases the total loss because the company recovers less in revenue than it spends on variable costs to produce that unit. Scaling volume magnifies this per-unit loss across more units, making the cumulative loss larger, not smaller. Fixed cost spreading only works when contribution margin is positive — in that case, higher volume allows fixed costs to be allocated across more profitable units. With negative contribution margin, there is no mechanism by which growth leads to profitability.

Why the others are wrong:

A) This confuses the role of fixed costs. Fixed cost leverage (spreading fixed costs over more units) only reduces per-unit total cost if the unit is profitable at the contribution margin level. A negative contribution margin means the company is already underwater on every unit before any fixed costs enter the calculation. Scaling worsens the problem.

C) This introduces price as a rescue variable, but the question states the company has negative contribution margins now — meaning revenue is already below variable costs. Raising prices in the future does not fix the current economics and relies on assumptions outside the unit economics model. The question asks whether the current strategy (scaling with negative margins) works.

D) This is a survivorship bias error. Successful startups were unprofitable because they were investing heavily in fixed costs (R&D, marketing, infrastructure) while already earning a positive contribution margin on each unit sold. They scaled a profitable unit into a profitable business. A company with negative contribution margin is not in this position and cannot be compared to that pattern.

Intuition: Contribution margin is the foundation of unit economics. No amount of operational leverage or volume can overcome a negative unit-level cash generation. Before scaling, a founder or analyst must ensure the basic unit economics are positive — that each sale contributes more revenue than variable cost. This is a non-negotiable screen in equity research and startup evaluation.
